placement.position_note: Interpretive placement on a GENERATED lot, not a recovered parcel. The lot geometry is the K7 plat module's — this project has never read Thompson's numbering off a sheet, and the side lot lines and the alley are conjectural even where the block face is not. M' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 4 — dated 1835-07-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. persons.name: Ebenezer Goodrich
persons.note: A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER OF 1833-1835 PRINTS THIS PERSON BY NAME IN THE TOWN. Read from newspaper_1833_1835, poll_1834. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_1833_1835 names this person at Chicago by 4 March 1834 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 1 time, as “GOODRICH EBENEZER”, 1833-10-22: 1 parcel of the school section — lot 1 of block 93 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $100.00 (ls0168). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: GOODRICH EBENEZER matches Ebenezer Goodrich: the forename names Ebenezer Goodrich of the 3 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Goodrich, Ebenezer” (poll_1834_045, line 214). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Goodrich' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

Temple, who had arrived early in July, 1833, with his family, consisting of a wife and four children. He was a pious and earnest Baptist Christian, and came to Chicago from Washington, D. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Temple, John T.” (poll_1833_027, line 48); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Temple, John” (tax_1833_102, line 154); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Temple, John T.” (poll_1834_107, line 276). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Temple' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 10 times, as “TEMPLE JOHN T”, “TEMPLE J T”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-21: 2 lots in the platted town — lot 4 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L4BL20CHIOT, as printed); lot 6 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L6BL20CHIOT, as printed) and 8 parcels of the school section — BL103 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL110 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL111 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL112 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL17 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL76 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL77 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL99 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read, 30.31 acres stated in all, for $21107.00 (ls0353, ls0354, ls0355, ls0356, ls0357, ls0358, ls0359, ls0360, ls1505, ls1506). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $20000.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: TEMPLE JOHN T matches Dr John Taylor Temple: the forename names Dr John Taylor Temple of the 3 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

persons.name: Mrs Temple
persons.note: DOCUMENTED AS A PERSON AND UNNAMED IN THE SOURCE. Andreas counts her - 'his family, consisting of a wife and four children' - and never gives her name. She is written as a person because the source counts her; the record carries no forename because inventing one would be the exact failure this grade exists to prevent.

persons.name: The four Temple children
persons.note: FOUR CHILDREN, COUNTED AND NOT NAMED. Andreas gives the number and nothing else - no names, no sexes, no ages. They are carried as one entry with a count in its name rather than as four invented individuals; the count is the evidence and the individuation is not. A later parcel with a church register or a school list would split this into four person records.

persons.name: Dr Peter Temple
persons.note: DOCUMENTED IN THE TOWN, DERIVED INTO THIS HOUSEHOLD. His own advertisement of 7 July 1834 places him 'adjacent to the dwelling of Dr. J. T. Temple' - i.e. NEXT DOOR, not in the same house - so grouping him here is a reconstruction and the note has to say so. He is also documented at Chicago after the scene date: on the executive committee of the Chicago Bible Society on 23 August 1835 and a secretary of the canal meeting of 7 November 1835. The brotherhood is Andreas's word ('through the influence of his brother') in a later passage.

residents.research_note: THE MODEL HOUSEHOLD FOR THIS PROGRAMME, because one sentence of Andreas supplies four of the six things K1 asks for - month of arrival, party size, origin and reason - and because the household then demonstrates the two honest ways of handling people a source counts but does not name. A wife who is counted gets a person record with no forename; four children who are counted get ONE record whose name states the count. Neither is inflated into individuals and neither is dropped. FIVE PERSONS ARE WRITTEN AND SIX PEOPLE ARE CLAIMED - the discrepancy is the four-children entry and it is deliberate; any later code that counts persons must read the notes, not the array length.

residents.name: The Timothv household — a name from the post office's letter lists
residents.why: boarding in the division's least crowded dwelling
residents.basis: HOUSED HERE BY THE DEAL, NOT RECORDED HERE (L354). This household was present in the town on 1 July 1835 and no source says where it slept; the roof is the invention and the people are not. Their card carries their evidence and is not touched by the seat.

persons.name: Pitkin Timothv
persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Pitkin Timothv' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 1 July 1835, column 5 — dated 1835-07-01. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1).

residents.research_note: MINTED FROM THE LETTER LISTS (T-0378, T-0379). THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER, NOT AN ARGUMENT: every other record here argues for a household, and this one argues for a PERSON. `data/residents/` cannot carry a person outside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing — one member, no dwelling, no division, no trade, no family, no arrival beyond the paper's bound. tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py derives the set and prints every refusal, `--gate` proves no record here gained a roof, a trade or a second member, and docs/LIBERTIES.md L214 carries the change of scale.

citations.citation: The baptismal register of St Mary's, Chicago — the first Catholic parish in the town — opened by Father John Mary Irenaeus St. Cyr on 22 May 1833 and read here for the years 1833, 1834 and 1835: 57 entries in French and English naming children, parents, godparents and witnesses, with the priest's own signature under every one and eight autographs of the town's own people beside them.

transcribes.work: The baptismal register kept at Chicago by Father J. M. I. St. Cyr from May 1833
transcribes.note: THE ORIGINAL, and these eleven images are photographs of it. A reading made off them is scan_verified — the higher of this project's two reading grades — and it outranks the marriage and death pages of st_cyr_register_ichr_v4, which reached this project through a 1921-22 article and a web transcription.

what_it_supplies: 57 dated baptisms of 1833-1835 and 267 named readings of people — 46 of the entries at Chicago and 166 of the readings adults there
KINSHIP, which no other source this project holds gives at all: a child, its two parents and its two godparents on one dated line, 44 times over
the town's Catholic population — French, Métis, Irish and German — of whom 85 distinct adults reach no surname in the residents layer

eight AUTOGRAPHS: Mark Beaubien, Josette Laframboise, Augustin Bonné, Monique Nadeau, Jean Baptiste Lavigne, J. B. Beaubien, Robert A. Kinzie and Gwinthlean Whistler signing under the priest, each placing a named person at a named place on a named day in their own hand
two adult baptisms with AGES — Josette Laframboise Beaubien at 38 in June 1834 and Geneviève Medera at about 20 in June 1835 — which are the only ages this project has for either woman
the parish's own start date, 22 May 1833, on a page the book heads '1er Page'
the register's own arithmetic: pencil tallies of 19, 24 and 14 baptisms for 1833, 1834 and 1835, which check any reading of it
a hue and cry on the title page describing what a young man of the Illinois country wore in 1833 or 1834 — a white pea coat, gray pants and a fur cap
what_it_does_not_supply: any address, lot, street, dwelling or workplace — the register places nobody anywhere in the town, and names no church building on any of the eleven pages
residence, and this is the trap. A baptism documents a person at a font on a day. Presence is not residence and nothing here mints or regrades a resident
presence on 1 July 1835 for anyone not baptised or standing as sponsor within days of it
occupation. One entry writes 'Doctor Egan' — a title inside a name — and that is the only trade the book ever states

ALL CHICAGO. Entries 1-11 of 1834 were written at Bear Creek, the South Fork of the Sangamon and Springfield, in Sangamon County, on the priest's journey back from St. Louis. A reader who takes the book as a Chicago roll plants eleven households in the wrong county
reliable spelling. A French priest wrote Irish, English and German names and phoneticised Potawatomi and Odawa ones; the same woman is Nadeau, Nodeau and Nodou in his own hand on three pages
the sponsors of 1834 entry 4, which stood on a line the scan's frame cuts off
anything about 1836 or later. The two page-sides in the deposit that carry 1837-38 and 1849 entries are declared and not transcribed
